lesson.menu_desc: Strong, soft and partial opinions -- I am convinced / I would say / that is a fair point, but -- 28 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 21 — Expressing Opinions with Confidence
lesson.title_tag: Professor View — Vanessa Giuriati | Lesson 21 — Expressing Opinions with Confidence
lesson.grammar_point: hedging and boosting opinions (I am convinced / I would say / I am not so sure)

listenings.text: Here is something I learned about giving opinions at work. For a long time I said yes to everything, because I was afraid of sounding difficult. Then a manager told me something simple: an opinion is information, not an attack. Now, when I disagree, I start with what I accept. That is a fair point, I say, and then I add my view. If I am completely sure, I say I am convinced, and I explain why. If I am not, I say I would say, or it depends, and nobody treats it as a promise. The hardest part is admitting when I am wrong. I still hate it. But the moment I admit it, the conversation moves forward instead of going in circles. So here is my advice. Do not confuse a strong opinion with a loud one. Say what you think, say how sure you are, and leave the door open for the other person.

I want to talk about the difference between an opinion and an assumption, because in meetings people mix them all the time. An opinion is what you think after looking at something. An assumption is what you believe before looking at anything. Both sound the same out loud, and that is the problem. Here is a test I use. Ask yourself: what would make me change my mind? If you can answer that question, you are holding an opinion. If nothing would change your mind, you are holding an assumption, and the discussion is already over. I am doubtful about people who are never doubtful. The strongest speakers I know are the ones who say I am convinced and mean it, but who also say I could be wrong about this part. That is not weakness. That is precision. Say clearly how sure you are, and people will trust the rest of what you say.

extra_audio.text: First, I listen and find one part of the other person's idea that I can accept. Then I say that it is a fair point, so the other person knows I was listening. After that, I give my own opinion and say how sure I am about it. Next, I explain the reason behind it, with one clear example. In the end, I ask what would change their mind, and I admit it if they are right.
